about: The studies the goal-set cards and the guided drills name, as read on the date given. A card may state only what is here: tests/node/evidence-ledger.test.mjs holds the cards to it.

levels.controlled: a trial with a comparison group, allocation not stated as random
levels.dose-comparison: a randomised comparison of doses with no untreated group
levels.single-case: a few people, each compared with their own baseline

sources.cite: Apfelbach CS, Guzmán M. Acoustic, Aerodynamic, Morphometric, and Perceptual Changes During and After Semi-Occluded Vocal Tract Exercise: An Integrative Review. J Voice 2024;38(2):404-425.
sources.population: Vocally untrained adults with and without dysphonia
sources.finding: 53 articles. Semi-occluded exercises reduce phonation threshold pressure and perceived phonatory effort.
sources.limits: Few studies examined how long the changes last after exercise; several trials support sustained effects with regular practice. Singers and trained voices are outside its scope. It does not test warming up before speaking or singing.

sources.cite: Whitling S, Wan Q, Berardi ML, Hunter EJ. Effects of warm-up exercises on self-assessed vocal effort. Logoped Phoniatr Vocol 2023;48(4):172-179.
sources.population: 26 vocally healthy adults in two randomised groups (reading aloud or semi-occluded exercises)
sources.finding: After a 5-minute warm-up, self-rated vocal effort rose in both groups; after 5 minutes of silence it was back at baseline.
sources.limits: Self-rating only. No group without a warm-up.

sources.cite: Kapsner-Smith MR, Hunter EJ, Kirkham K, Cox K, Titze IR. A Randomized Controlled Trial of Two Semi-Occluded Vocal Tract Voice Therapy Protocols. J Speech Lang Hear Res 2015;58(3):535-549.
sources.population: 20 adults with hoarseness or vocal fatigue
sources.finding: Flow-resistant tube therapy and vocal function exercises both improved self-reported voice handicap against delayed therapy.
sources.limits: Patients, not healthy speakers. All four tube exercises (glide, accents, songs, 'reading' a paragraph without articulation) are done through the straw: the programme has no step of speaking without it. Outcomes are for the whole programme.
sources.by: independent checker (abstract); author (full text, a third-party copy read through a page summariser, because PubMed Central refused automated access)

sources.cite: Peng J, Zou M, Ng ML, Hou Q, Zhu L, Tan J, Zhang Q. The impact and application exercises on vocal fatigue. Sci Rep 2026;16(1):22790.
sources.population: 114 healthy adults after one hour of vocal loading, three groups
sources.finding: Five minutes of rest then five of straw phonation gave better acoustic measures and lower self-rated discomfort and effort than ten minutes of rest alone.
sources.limits: One study. Measured once, straight after the ten minutes; no later follow-up. Prevention was not tested.

sources.cite: Hunter EJ, Titze IR. Quantifying vocal fatigue recovery: dynamic vocal recovery trajectories after a vocal loading exercise. Ann Otol Rhinol Laryngol 2009;118(6):449-460.
sources.population: 86 adults after 2 hours of oral reading
sources.finding: About 90% of recovery within 4 to 6 hours, full recovery at 12 to 18 hours.
sources.limits: Self-tracked short tasks and ratings. Not a safe daily dose.

sources.cite: Picheny MA, Durlach NI, Braida LD. Speaking clearly for the hard of hearing I: Intelligibility differences between clear and conversational speech. J Speech Hear Res 1985;28(1):96-103.
sources.population: 5 listeners with sensorineural hearing loss, 3 talkers, nonsense sentences
sources.finding: Clear speech was understood 17 percentage points better than conversational speech.
sources.limits: A laboratory result about the listener. Not a training study.

sources.cite: Smiljanić R, Bradlow AR. Speaking and Hearing Clearly: Talker and Listener Factors in Speaking Style Changes. Lang Linguist Compass 2009;3(1):236-264.
sources.population: Review of clear-speech production and perception
sources.finding: The clear-speech benefit holds for several listener groups and in noise.
sources.limits: A narrative review. It does not measure what home practice teaches.

sources.cite: Rosenberg A, Hirschberg J. Acoustic/prosodic and lexical correlates of charismatic speech. Interspeech 2005.
sources.population: 8 native speakers of American English rated 45 clips from 9 political candidates
sources.finding: Clips with a higher mean pitch and a larger spread of pitch were rated more charismatic.
sources.limits: A correlation in ratings of American political speech; the authors say the analysis is not complete and hesitate to generalise.
sources.by: author (the authors' copy, read through a page summariser; the independent checker reached only the bibliographic record)

sources.cite: Hincks R, Edlund J. Promoting Increased Pitch Variation in Oral Presentations with Transient Visual Feedback. Language Learning & Technology 2009 (October issue).
sources.population: 14 Chinese learners of English in two groups, presenting in a second language
sources.finding: Both groups varied pitch more with training; the group with a visual signal of pitch variation increased it more than the group with audio feedback.
sources.limits: Small, second-language speakers. It does not show listeners prefer the result.

sources.cite: Luiselli JK. Public speaking disfluencies: A review of habit reversal training and research. J Appl Behav Anal 2022;55(4):1342-1348.
sources.population: Review of 7 single-case studies in one journal, 2016 to 2022
sources.finding: Seven studies evaluated habit reversal (awareness training, with or without a competing response) for filled pauses in public speaking.
sources.limits: Its abstract gives no pooled outcome. The seven study abstracts were read one by one (PMIDs 26947580, 27766654, 31032933, 31475352, 33155271, 34289092, 34545944): each reports fewer fillers, in 4 to 9 people, most of them university students.

sources.cite: Mancuso C, Miltenberger RG. Using habit reversal to decrease filled pauses in public speaking. J Appl Behav Anal 2016;49(1):188-192.
sources.population: 6 participants
sources.finding: After awareness training and competing response training, all 6 showed an immediate decrease in filled pauses.
sources.limits: No comparison group. The abstract does not say what the competing response was; the thesis copy refused automated access.

sources.cite: Pawlik B, Perrin CJ. Reducing speech disfluencies during public speaking using brief habit reversal. J Appl Behav Anal 2020;53(2):1080-1088.
sources.population: 4 participants
sources.finding: Awareness training plus an instructed silent pause: all 4 reduced disfluencies; 1 used the pause at moderate levels.
sources.limits: No comparison group. The pause itself was little used. Perrin et al. 2021 (PMID 34289092, 9 students) found the same: the pause stayed high for 1 participant.

sources.cite: Stemple JC, Lee L, D'Amico B, Pickup B. Efficacy of vocal function exercises as a method of improving voice production. J Voice 1994;8(3):271-278.
sources.population: 35 adult women with normal voice, randomly divided into exercise, placebo and control groups
sources.finding: After 4 weeks, maximum phonation time, frequency range, phonation volume and flow rate changed significantly only in the exercise group.
sources.limits: Women only, four weeks. Measures of voice function, not of everyday speech.

sources.cite: Sabol JW, Lee L, Stemple JC. The value of vocal function exercises in the practice regimen of singers. J Voice 1995;9(1):27-36.
sources.population: 20 healthy graduate voice majors, 10 exercising and 10 not
sources.finding: After 4 weeks, flow rate, phonation volume and maximum phonation time improved in the exercise group.
sources.limits: The abstract says 'divided' and does not state random allocation. No rating of how the singing sounds.

sources.cite: Bane M, Angadi V, Dressler E, Andreatta R, Stemple J. Vocal function exercises for normal voice: The effects of varying dosage. Int J Speech Lang Pathol 2019;21(1):37-45.
sources.population: 28 women aged 18 to 25 with normal voice, three doses
sources.finding: Six weeks, twice daily. Each exercise twice per session improved maximum phonation time significantly; once per session gave a smaller gain that was not significant.
sources.limits: No untreated or placebo group: it compares doses, so it is not a controlled trial of the exercises against nothing.

sources.cite: Angadi V, Croake D, Stemple J. Effects of Vocal Function Exercises: A Systematic Review. J Voice 2019;33(1):124.e13-124.e34.
sources.population: 21 studies of normal and disordered voices
sources.finding: None of the included studies reported adverse voice outcomes.
sources.limits: No study reported harm; that is not the same as harm being monitored. Shares an author with the 1994 and 1995 trials.

sources.cite: Ruotsalainen JH, Sellman J, Lehto L, Jauhiainen M, Verbeek JH. Interventions for preventing voice disorders in adults. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2007;(4):CD006372.
sources.population: 2 randomised trials in teachers and student teachers (53 and 43 participants)
sources.finding: No evidence that voice training prevents voice disorders.
sources.limits: Two small, poor-quality trials, searched to 2006; none counted diagnosed disorders. Absence of good evidence, not evidence of no effect.

sources.cite: Ramos LA, Ribeiro CJS, Brasil CCP, Gama ACC. The Effectiveness of Vocal Health Programs in the Prevention of Voice Disorders in Teachers: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. J Voice 2025;39(2):564.e1-564.e21.
sources.population: 26 studies of school teachers without vocal complaints, 12 pooled
sources.finding: No pooled effect on voice handicap, phonation time or acoustic measures; the authors say the results allow no conclusion.
sources.limits: No study at low risk of bias. Surrogate measures, not counts of voice disorders.

sources.cite: Moorcroft L, Kenny DT. Singer and listener perception of vocal warm-up. J Voice 2013;27(2):258.e1-258.e13.
sources.population: 12 classically trained female singers; 6 experienced listeners
sources.finding: After a 25-minute warm-up all singers perceived changes; most listeners heard a difference only for singers whose vibrato became more moderate.
sources.limits: Before and after, no control condition.

sources.cite: Berglin J, Pfordresher PQ, Demorest S. The effect of visual and auditory feedback on adult poor-pitch remediation. Psychology of Music 2022;50(4):1077-1090.
sources.population: Adult poor-pitch singers, three randomised 20-minute conditions
sources.finding: Gains were greater with visual feedback plus hearing the target than with auditory-only practice or a control task.
sources.limits: One session, tested straight after, no follow-up. The abstract gives no sample size.

sources.cite: Paney AS, Tharp KL. The effect of concurrent visual feedback on adult singing accuracy. Psychology of Music 2021;49(3):360-370.
sources.population: University students not majoring in music, two randomised groups, 10 weeks
sources.finding: Both groups improved; the group with concurrent visual feedback did not score significantly higher than the group without it.
sources.limits: Small; the practice tool was a game.

sources.cite: Ragan K. The Impact of Vocal Cool-down Exercises: A Subjective Study of Singers' and Listeners' Perceptions. J Voice 2016;30(6):764.e1-764.e9.
sources.population: 20 classically trained female singers after a 60-minute voice load; 4 expert listeners
sources.finding: 68%, 67% and 74% reported improvement on three questionnaires; the improvement was not statistically significant; listeners picked the cool-down week 46% of the time.
sources.limits: Self-report and listener judgement only; nothing was measured instrumentally.

sources.cite: Vermeulen R, du Toit M, van Lierde K, van der Linde J. The Effect of Vocal Hygiene Education Programs on Voice Quality in Professional Voice Users: A Systematic Review. J Speech Lang Hear Res 2022;65(12):4700-4713.
sources.population: 23 studies of professional voice users
sources.finding: 10 of 23 studies linked voice training or hygiene education to positive voice outcomes; results were mixed.
sources.limits: Voice quality and function, not counts of diagnosed disorders.

sources.cite: Meerschman I, Van Lierde K, Peeters K, Meersman E, Claeys S, D'haeseleer E. Short-Term Effect of Two Semi-Occluded Vocal Tract Training Programs on the Vocal Quality of Future Occupational Voice Users. J Speech Lang Hear Res 2017;60(9):2519-2536.
sources.population: 30 healthy speech-language pathology students, 10 per group, 6 weeks
sources.finding: No significant difference between resonant voice training, straw phonation and no training.
sources.limits: The null covers straw phonation as well as resonant voice; ten per group cannot rule out an effect. Each trained group improved on one measure.

sources.cite: Nanjundeswaran C, Li NY, Chan KM, Wong RK, Yiu EM, Verdolini-Abbott K. Preliminary data on prevention and treatment of voice problems in student teachers. J Voice 2012;26(6):816.e1-12.
sources.population: 31 student teachers in three groups
sources.finding: In healthy participants a hygiene programme stopped the worsening of voice handicap seen in controls; adding resonant voice training gave no consistent extra benefit; it helped those who already had problems.
sources.limits: Preliminary, descriptive, self-reported.

sources.cite: Bane M, Angadi V, Andreatta R, Stemple J. The Effect of Maximum Phonation Time Goal on Efficacy of Vocal Function Exercises. J Voice 2025;39(5):1254-1261.
sources.population: 19 completers with normal voice, three groups
sources.finding: The authors conclude the time goal is an active ingredient.
sources.limits: The confidence intervals of the group differences cross zero.

sources.cite: Bane M, Morton M, Angadi V, Andreatta R, Stemple J. Vocal Function Exercises With and Without Maximally Sustained Phonation: A Randomized Controlled Trial of Individuals With Normal Voice. J Voice 2025;39(2):410-417.
sources.population: 23 completers with normal voice
sources.finding: Removing the maximal sustain may attenuate improvement.
sources.limits: The difference between groups was not statistically significant.

sources.cite: Spieler C, Miltenberger R. Using awareness training to decrease nervous habits during public speaking. J Appl Behav Anal 2017;50(1):38-47.
sources.population: 4 university students
sources.finding: Awareness training alone reduced filled pauses for all four; booster sessions were needed.
sources.limits: No comparison group; no competing response was taught.

sources.cite: Laske MM, DiGennaro Reed FD, Braren JTB. The efficacy of remote video-based behavioral skills training and awareness training on public speaking performance. J Appl Behav Anal 2024;57(1):247-261.
sources.population: 2 participants
sources.finding: Awareness training reduced disfluencies, but expert ratings of speaking effectiveness did not improve and some worsened.
sources.limits: Two people. Fewer fillers did not make experts rate the talk better.

sources.cite: Barsties v. Latoszek B, Watts CR, Schwan K, Hetjens S. The maximum phonation time as marker for voice treatment efficacy: a network meta-analysis. Clin Otolaryngol 2023;48(2):130-138.
sources.population: 12 randomised trials in adults with voice disorders
sources.finding: Vocal function exercises were the only intervention with a significant effect on maximum phonation time.
sources.limits: Patients only; healthy voices were excluded.
